rv.q: Few playwrights are examining what Akhtar does, certainly not with his insightfulness, and his play is breathtaking — and not a little uncomfortable — to watch.
Mr. Akhtar’s play has come roaring back to life on Broadway in a first-rate production directed by Kimberly Senior that features an almost entirely new cast.
Mr. Akhtar has written a smart, savage play about the impossibility of escaping from your past, and Ms. Patel has staged it with unflinching honesty.
Happily, the structure, as precisely crafted as the kind of Swiss watch Amir might sport, mostly survives translation.
In truth, this is a superior production to the one that opened at Lincoln Center in 2012, with a more charismatic cast.
That willingness to embrace such complexity is what makes "Disgraced" such an unstinting and immediate drama, likely now to reach a much wider audience.

Akhtar, providing in Shavian style a spectrum of lively, contentious perspectives, inspires a provocative consideration of the matrix of personal choices and social pitfalls that a member of any religious minority, and in this case, a Muslim, may confront in this country.
If Disgraced has sacrificed some of its edge in the move to a commercial mainstage, it’s nonetheless a stimulating, sobering work from a distinctive new American playwright.
It’s a more classical approach, a study of a powerful man destroyed by hubris.
Too bad Broadway doesn't get to feel all the burn.
That's the power and the problem of Disgraced: Its punches are shockingly believable.
This little off-Broadway potboiler has reduced to a simmer in the move to Times Square.
But the bigger stage hasn’t been kind to the show.

There are some topics you just shouldn't discuss at a dinner party. Religion, race, politics -- it's probably good to avoid these controversial matters altogether, and focus on more agreeable subjects. Like the weather. Perhaps if the two couples in 'Disgraced' would have taken that advice, they would have avoided a whole lot of trouble and pain.
It’s as if he didn’t want to dwell too long on the crash site he had orchestrated for his flawed and deeply human characters.
By making us examine several such hard issues, Disgraced succeeds despite a few structural flaws.
Even if some of the plot developments are relatively over-the-top, Akhtar raises a provocative debate over racial and religious identity that is as compelling as it is disturbing.
Ayad Akhtar's 90-minute drama about the role of religion, politics and identity in our terror-ridden world has flaws but it is extremely provocative.
It’s baffling and more than a little unsatisfying to have a minor character undergo the play’s greatest metamorphosis and to do so offstage when the major characters are fighting it out onstage.
Blunted by contrivances, the impact of "Disgraced" isn't as sharp — or as potentially dangerous — as it could be.
Their combined efforts make Disgraced consistently entertaining and thought-provoking -- just not as much as you wish it were.
They lack the nuggets of lumps and bumps that make people unique.

cn.t: Akhtar's Pulitzer-winning drama earns praise for its provocative, unflinching exploration of identity and prejudice in post-9/11 America, though some critics fault its didactic structure and convenient plotting.

sg.ra: Center orchestra rows D-G offer head-on sightlines to the high stage without neck strain. Gentle rake; intimate 922-seat house means even mid-orchestra feels close. Playbill notes Oh, Mary! action is downstage center, rewarding central seats.

Telecharge lists extreme sides of the first 11 orchestra rows as obstructed-view seats per Playbill. SeatPlan confirms double-digit seats are angled with far-side stage obstruction. 1903 house geometry leaves sharp side angles near stage.

sg.n: Orchestra Rear (Rows L-O, behind mezz overhang)
sg.ra: TickPick and SeatPlan both confirm Mezzanine overhang begins at Row L of Orchestra. AVFMS reviewer for O12 praised tiered rake ('raised above the row in front so you don't have any heads blocking you'). Fine for plays; top-of-stage cutoff limits tall-set musicals.

SeatPlan: 'patrons can look directly down to the stage, taking advantage of the Mezzanine's fantastic aerial views which don't sacrifice detail.' Excellent rake prevents blocked views. Ideal for spectacle/musicals where staging composition matters.

Folliesbroadway and Headout both flag Mezz D-F center as best value: clean sightlines, excellent rake, priced materially below front-mezz/prime-orchestra. Balcony overhang doesn't cut in until Row C so D-F also sit past the cutoff line without being affected (SeatPlan note is about row C).

sg.n: Mezzanine Rear (behind Row C — balcony overhang) and Side Double-Digits
sg.ra: SeatPlan: 'Balcony overhang kicks in at row C, so views behind this may experience cut-off at the top of the stage.' Double-digit side seats (D24, G22) have partial sightlines. Fine for plays; poor for tall scenic musicals.

Rows B and C clear the Row A safety rail and preserve a steep but clean center view. Tripadvisor: 'Great view of the stage, although a bit of an angled view down.' Starting prices on SeatPlan as low as $68-$80. Steep rake is uncomfortable but preserves sightlines.

sg.n: Balcony Row A and Side L/R front rows
sg.ra: Row A front has a safety rail that cuts across the stage (SeatPlan, Playbill, Tripadvisor all independently confirm). TickPick: Balcony L and R first two rows have partial views due to railing. Shorter patrons especially affected.
